title: DOW-UAP-D085_Transmission-of-CIA-Scientific-Advisory-Panel-Rept_1953
what_is_it: Cover letter and routing slip transmitting the CIA's 1953 Scientific Advisory Panel report on Unidentified Flying Objects (the Robertson Panel report) to the Secretary of Defense.
core_summary: This document is a classified CIA transmittal dated 17 March 1953 forwarding the report of a scientific panel convened to evaluate Unidentified Flying Objects. The cover letter, signed by Richard D. Drain of the Intelligence Advisory Committee, states the panel was convened at the direction of General Smith and notes that its conclusions point out potential dangers to national security related to the UFO subject. The panel concluded that UFOs posed no direct physical threat to national security but warned of indirect dangers such as the clogging of communication channels.
interpretation_warnings: OCR quality is extremely poor throughout — most of the attached panel report (pages 3, 5, 6, 7) is nearly illegible, with only scattered words recoverable.
The bulk of the scientific panel's actual findings, evidence review, and detailed recommendations are unreadable due to degraded source quality, not formal redaction.
Only the cover letter (page 4) and routing slip (page 2) are substantially legible.
This is the transmittal copy, not the full Robertson Panel report itself; the attached report pages are too degraded to extract substantive content.
The document was classified under US espionage laws at time of creation.

public_headline: CIA Sent Its 1953 UFO Panel Report to the Secretary of Defense
public_tldr: This 1953 document is a CIA cover letter forwarding the Robertson Panel's scientific report on Unidentified Flying Objects to the Secretary of Defense. The panel found UFOs posed no direct physical threat but warned that UFO reports could clog military communication channels — an indirect national security risk.
public_narrative:
On 17 March 1953, the CIA transmitted a scientific panel's report on Unidentified Flying Objects — also referred to as "Flying Saucers" — to the Secretary of Defense. The cover letter was signed by Richard D. Drain of the Intelligence Advisory Committee. According to the letter, the panel had been convened at the direction of General Smith, following a recommendation by the Intelligence Advisory Committee.

The panel's key conclusion, as described in the cover letter, was that UFOs did not pose a direct physical threat to national security. However, the panel warned of indirect dangers — specifically, that a flood of UFO sighting reports could clog communication channels, potentially interfering with military operations. The panel suggested ways to eliminate these indirect risks.

The CIA's cover letter also made clear that the agency did not consider UFO sightings to be primarily its concern, though it offered to assist. Copies of the report were also sent to the Chairman of the National Security Resources Board.

The document was classified under US espionage laws (Title 18, Sections 793 and 794) at the time of its creation. What survives today is the transmittal copy — a routing slip and cover letter — rather than the full panel report itself. The attached pages of the actual scientific panel report are nearly illegible due to severe degradation of the source material.

This is an important distinction: most of the panel's detailed findings, evidence review, and specific recommendations cannot be read from this copy. The illegibility stems from poor document quality rather than formal redaction, though the document also shows evidence of heavy redaction throughout.
public_caveats: This is the transmittal copy (cover letter and routing slip), not the full Robertson Panel report — the actual panel findings attached are nearly illegible due to source degradation.
OCR quality is extremely poor on most pages; only the cover letter and routing slip are substantially readable.
Heavy redaction is present throughout the document, separate from the degradation issues.

The panel's conclusion that UFOs posed 'no direct physical threat' and the concern about 'clogging communication channels' are only partially legible in the source text and should be treated with moderate confidence.
The document was classified under espionage laws when created; its current availability does not mean all contents are recoverable or complete.
